attr   <- readRDS(here::here(DIR_DERIVED, "country_attribution.rds"))

ret    <- readRDS(here::here(DIR_DERIVED, "retrieval_ledger.rds"))

contest<- readRDS(here::here(DIR_DERIVED, "contested_set.rds"))

  dplyr::distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE)

GREY_TYPES <- c("dissertation", "report", "preprint", "book-chapter", "book",
                "conference-paper", "conference-abstract", "other")

map <- tiers |>
  dplyr::filter(analytic) |>
  dplyr::select(id, title, tier, study_country, type) |>
  dplyr::left_join(attr |> dplyr::select(id, dplyr::all_of(COUNTRIES),
                                         n_countries, any_country,
                                         quote_grounded, dplyr::ends_with("_named")),
                   by = "id") |>
  dplyr::left_join(ledg |> dplyr::select(id, publication_year, is_oa, doi,
                                         provenance_sources, provenance_cells, n_merged),
                   by = "id") |>
  dplyr::left_join(ret |> dplyr::select(id, tei_ok), by = "id") |>
  dplyr::left_join(auth |> dplyr::select(id, n_authors, author_countries,
                                         first_incountry, last_incountry, any_incountry),
                   by = "id") |>
  dplyr::left_join(conf |> dplyr::select(id, max_confidence, min_confidence), by = "id") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    contested = id %in% contest$id,
    stratum   = dplyr::if_else(type %in% GREY_TYPES | is.na(type), "grey", "peer-reviewed"),
    sources   = vapply(provenance_sources,
                       function(x) paste(sort(unique(unlist(x))), collapse = "+"), character(1)),
    n_cells   = lengths(provenance_cells))
n_map <- NROW(map)

1 What this map claims, and what it cannot

This is an automated evidence map, not a scoping review. It makes claims about the distribution of research — across countries, taxa, conflict types and methods — not about a precisely bounded included set. That distinction is what makes it defensible under a pipeline with no human reviewer: if classification errors are not systematically biased by country or taxon, a distributional claim survives them, while a boundary claim would not.

Four constraints shape everything below and are repeated at each point they bite rather than confined to a limitations paragraph:

  1. English-indexed literature only. Search and screening were English-language only. French and Arabic query cells were executed but returned 2 and 0 records respectively, reflecting narrower non-English term blocks rather than an absence of literature. Evidence gaps reported here are gaps in English-indexed literature.
  2. 121 of 262 records have full text. Fields requiring the methods or results section are reported over that stratum with its own denominator.
  3. Counts by country are not mutually exclusive. A study covering three countries counts in three cells.
  4. Absence in this map is absence of retrieved, screened, English-indexed evidence. Where that is distinguishable from a real research gap, the text says which it is. Where it is not, it says that too.

2 From search to map: the record arithmetic

# The canonical flow, built and reconciled once in R/build_record_flow.R so
# that this module and the Module 08 diagram cannot disagree.
flow <- readr::read_csv(here::here(DIR_DERIVED, "record_flow.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
geo  <- readRDS(here::here(DIR_DERIVED, "geography_verification.rds"))
n_retrieved <- flow$n[flow$step == 1]
knitr::kable(flow |> dplyr::select(stage, n, removed, removal_reason),
             caption = "From retrieval to the analytic set")
From retrieval to the analytic set
stage n removed removal_reason
Records retrieved (OpenAlex + CORE, all cells) 95546 NA NA
After deduplication 65820 29726 duplicate records merged
Abstract present, eligible for screening 61065 4755 no abstract: DEFERRED, not excluded
Screened by the ensemble 60961 104 inference failed on every attempt: DEFERRED, not excluded
Included by the ensemble (union rule) 550 60411 judged not eligible by both models
Verified as located in the five countries 266 284 located outside the five countries

stopifnot(flow$n[flow$step == 7] == n_map)

The map rests on 262 records — 0.274% of the 95,546 the search retrieved. Each contraction is documented in its own module, and the largest are not equivalent: deduplication removed redundancy, whereas the geographic gate removed 284 records the classifier had wrongly included.

Two strata were deferred, not excluded — 4755 records with no abstract and 104 on which inference failed outright. They were never judged, and a flow that folded them into “excluded” would misstate what this pipeline did.

3 Geographic distribution

3.1 Raw counts

country_long <- map |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::all_of(COUNTRIES), names_to = "country", values_to = "covered") |>
  dplyr::filter(covered %in% TRUE)

geo_tbl <- tibble::tibble(country = COUNTRIES) |>
  dplyr::left_join(country_long |> dplyr::count(country, name = "studies"), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::left_join(country_long |> dplyr::filter(n_countries == 1) |>
                     dplyr::count(country, name = "sole_focus"), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::left_join(country_long |> dplyr::filter(stratum == "peer-reviewed") |>
                     dplyr::count(country, name = "peer_reviewed"), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::left_join(country_long |> dplyr::filter(stratum == "grey") |>
                     dplyr::count(country, name = "grey"), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::left_join(country_long |> dplyr::filter(tei_ok %in% TRUE) |>
                     dplyr::count(country, name = "with_full_text"), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(-country, ~ tidyr::replace_na(.x, 0L)))

59 of the 262 analytic records could not be attributed to any of the five countries from title and abstract. They passed the in-scope gate but name no country specifically enough to place. They are not distributed across the cells above, so every count here is a floor.

3.2 Normalised by land area and population

A raw count conflates “little research happens here” with “this is a small country”. Both denominators come from the World Bank (land area 2023, population 2025).

geo_norm <- geo_tbl |>
  dplyr::left_join(ctx |> dplyr::select(country, land_area_km2, population), by = "country") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    per_100k_km2 = round(studies / (land_area_km2 / 1e5), 2),
    per_million_people = round(studies / (population / 1e6), 2)) |>
  dplyr::select(country, studies, land_area_km2, population,
                per_100k_km2, per_million_people) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(studies))

rank_pop  <- geo_norm |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(per_million_people)) |> dplyr::pull(country)

The gap, quantified. Tunisia carries 81 studies and Libya carries 31 — a ratio of 2.6 to 1 in raw counts. Per 100,000 km² the spread widens sharply, from 52.14 (Tunisia) to 1.76 (Libya) — a ratio of 29.6 to 1, because the countries with the fewest studies are also the largest.

But the denominator changes the answer, and that has to be said. Per million people the order is different: Tunisia is highest at 6.56 and Egypt is lowest at 0.63.

knitr::kable(tibble::tibble(
  rank = seq_along(rank_raw),
  `by raw count` = rank_raw,
  `per 100,000 km²` = rank_area,
  `per million people` = rank_pop),
  caption = "Country order under each denominator")
Country order under each denominator
rank by raw count per 100,000 km² per million people
1 Tunisia Tunisia Tunisia
2 Morocco Morocco Libya
3 Egypt Egypt Morocco
4 Algeria Algeria Algeria
5 Libya Libya Egypt

Libya ranks 5th of 5 on raw count, 5th per unit area, and 2nd per million people. A country with a small population can look research-rich per capita while holding very few studies in absolute terms. Neither denominator is the right one on its own, and this map reports all three rather than choosing the one that tells the tidiest story. Where the three disagree, the raw count is what a researcher planning fieldwork needs and the normalised figures are what a funder allocating effort needs.

p <- geo_norm |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(studies, per_100k_km2, per_million_people),
                      names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  dplyr::mutate(measure = factor(measure, c("studies", "per_100k_km2", "per_million_people"),
                                 c("studies", "per 100,000 km²", "per million people"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(country, value), y = value, fill = measure)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_x") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = OKABE[c(6, 5, 3)]) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Human-wildlife conflict research across North Africa",
       subtitle = sprintf("%d studies; counts are not mutually exclusive", n_map)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
save_fig(p, "07_geographic_distribution", w = 8, h = 4.5)

3.3 Is a thin cell a gap, or an artefact?

art <- geo_tbl |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    ret |> dplyr::mutate(cell_country = country) |> dplyr::count(cell_country, name = "cell_records"),
    by = c("country" = "cell_country")) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    ret |> dplyr::group_by(cell_country = country) |>
      dplyr::summarise(cell_tei_pct = round(100 * mean(tei_ok %in% TRUE), 1), .groups = "drop"),
    by = c("country" = "cell_country")) |>
  dplyr::select(country, studies, cell_records, cell_tei_pct)
knitr::kable(art, caption = "Studies found against how much the search cell returned and how much of it was readable")
Studies found against how much the search cell returned and how much of it was readable
country studies cell_records cell_tei_pct
Tunisia 81 NA NA
Algeria 47 NA NA
Morocco 76 NA NA
Libya 31 NA NA
Egypt 75 NA NA

This table is the honest reading of the one above it. A country with few studies and a thin search cell and poor full-text retrieval has three compounding shortfalls, and the map cannot separate them from a genuine absence of research. Naming that country’s low count as a “research gap” without this table beside it would be the central failure mode of this study.

half <- yr |> dplyr::mutate(era = dplyr::if_else(publication_year >= 2015, "2015+", "pre-2015")) |>
  dplyr::count(era)

217 of 261 (83%) were published in 2015 or later. Read that as growth in indexed, English-language output as much as growth in research: OpenAlex coverage of regional journals improves sharply over the same period, and the two cannot be separated here.

tc <- country_long |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(publication_year), publication_year <= FUTURE) |>
  dplyr::count(country, publication_year, name = "n")

5 Language and indexing

idx <- tibble::tibble(
  quantity = c("records in the analytic set",
               "found via OpenAlex only", "found via CORE only", "found via both",
               "found by exactly one search cell",
               "open access flagged", "records in French or Arabic",
               "estimated in-scope works citation chasing would have added"),
  n = c(n_map,
        sum(map$sources == "openalex"), sum(map$sources == "core"),
        sum(map$sources == "core+openalex"),
        sum(map$n_cells == 1),
        sum(map$is_oa %in% TRUE),
        sum(ledg$language[ledg$id %in% map$id] %in% c("fr", "ar")),
        # Read from the probe's own stored estimate, never re-derived here.
        round(probe$estimate$estimate[probe$estimate$test == "strict"])))
knitr::kable(idx, caption = "How the analytic set was found")

##   quantity                                                       n
##   <chr>                                                      <dbl>
## 1 records in the analytic set                                  262
## 2 found via OpenAlex only                                      234
## 3 found via CORE only                                            8
## 4 found via both                                                20
## 5 found by exactly one search cell                             111
## 6 open access flagged                                          239
## 7 records in French or Arabic                                    0
## 8 estimated in-scope works citation chasing would have added     5

8 records came from CORE alone and would have been missed by an OpenAlex-only search; 111 of 262 (42%) were returned by exactly one search cell, so a single term-block change would have dropped them. That is a fragile search, and it is the strongest internal evidence that the absences in this map are partly artefacts of how it was built.

pe <- probe$estimate |> dplyr::filter(test == "strict")

The last row is the calibrated citation-probe estimate from Module 02b: approximately 5 in-scope works (95% CI 0–26) that backward and forward citation chasing would have added, against a 262-record analytic set. The interval is wide because the raw detection was 1 record and the string test’s measured sensitivity is only 0.217. That probe searches the citation neighbourhood of records we already found, so it bounds what citation chasing would have added — not what the search missed overall.

Zero records are in French or Arabic. The French cells returned 2 records across the entire 65,820-record corpus and the Arabic cells returned none. That is a term-coverage artefact — the non-English blocks were far narrower, and the Latin binomials that would have caught francophone papers sat in an English-filtered cell. Maghreb wildlife research is substantially francophone, so the Algerian and Moroccan cells in this map are the ones most likely to understate real research activity, and no count here should be read as evidence about the francophone literature.

6 Authorship equity

cov <- map |> dplyr::filter(!is.na(author_countries))
eq <- tibble::tibble(
  measure = c("first author in-country", "senior (last) author in-country",
              "any author in-country", "no in-country author"),
  n = c(sum(cov$first_incountry %in% TRUE), sum(cov$last_incountry %in% TRUE),
        sum(cov$any_incountry %in% TRUE), sum(cov$any_incountry %in% FALSE)),
  denominator = c(sum(!is.na(cov$first_incountry)), sum(!is.na(cov$last_incountry)),
                  sum(!is.na(cov$any_incountry)), sum(!is.na(cov$any_incountry)))) |>
  dplyr::mutate(pct = round(100 * n / denominator, 1))
knitr::kable(eq, caption = "In-country authorship, over records with affiliation metadata")

An author counts as in-country if any of their affiliations on that work sits in one of the five countries, which counts a Tunisian author with a joint French post as Tunisian. The generous reading makes the finding conservative: if the share is low even counting joint appointments, it is genuinely low.

7 Taxonomic, conflict type, and method

# The guard is the MANIFEST, not file existence. An earlier version of this
# chunk tested only that extraction_fields.rds existed; it passed on the
# output of a 5-record smoke run and this module published a taxonomic table
# reading "n = 4 studies" as though it described the corpus. A partial run
# must be indistinguishable from no run at all here.
man_path <- here::here(DIR_DERIVED, "extraction_manifest.rds")
ext_path <- here::here(DIR_DERIVED, "extraction_fields.rds")
rel_path <- here::here(DIR_TABLES, "extraction_reliability.csv")

man <- if (file.exists(man_path)) readRDS(man_path) else NULL
have_ext <- !is.null(man) && isTRUE(man$complete) &&
  file.exists(ext_path) && file.exists(rel_path) &&
  man$n_records >= 0.95 * n_map
if (!is.null(man)) knitr::kable(man, caption = "Module 06 extraction manifest")
Module 06 extraction manifest
when limit n_analytic n_records n_calls n_calls_ok n_calls_failed xmodel model xmodel_name complete
2026-08-24 03:19:22 NA 262 260 1716 1716 0 TRUE gemma4:e4b qwen2.5:7b TRUE 
ext <- readRDS(ext_path)
rel <- readr::read_csv(rel_path, show_col_types = FALSE)
unreliable <- rel$field[!rel$reliable %in% TRUE]
cat("Fields excluded from the headline analysis (below the",
    FIELD_RELIABILITY_MIN, "reliability floor):\n  ",
    paste(unreliable, collapse = ", "), "\n")
## Fields excluded from the headline analysis (below the 0.7 reliability floor):
##    damage_metric_reported, compensation_scheme_discussed, study_design, subnational_region, species_scientific
# FREE-TEXT NORMALISATION.
# The model returns species names as written in each paper, so one taxon
# arrives as "sea turtles", "sea turtle", "loggerhead turtle" and "loggerhead
# turtles". Counting those as four species understates every one of them and
# corrupts the taxonomic strand, which is the point of this section.
#
# Normalisation is deliberately conservative: lower-case, strip punctuation,
# collapse whitespace, and singularise a trailing "s" only on words longer
# than three characters whose ending is not itself part of the singular --
# "ss", "us", "is", "as", "os". Without the "is" guard this turned "northern
# bald ibis" into "ibi". It merges
# plurals; it does NOT merge "loggerhead turtle" into "sea turtle", because
# that is a taxonomic judgement and the model was not asked to make it. The
# raw-to-normalised mapping is printed so the merge can be audited.
.norm_species <- function(x) {
  y <- tolower(trimws(gsub("[[:punct:]]+", " ", x)))
  y <- gsub("\\s+", " ", y)
  vapply(strsplit(y, " "), function(w) {
    w <- vapply(w, function(t)
      if (nchar(t) > 3 && grepl("s$", t) && !grepl("(ss|us|is|as|os)$", t))
        sub("s$", "", t) else t, character(1))
    paste(w, collapse = " ")
  }, character(1))
}

.field_counts <- function(f, normalise = FALSE) {
  if (f %in% unreliable) return(NULL)
  d <- ext |> dplyr::filter(field == f, !is.na(value_final), value_final != "not stated")
  if (normalise) d <- d |> dplyr::mutate(value_final = .norm_species(value_final))
  d |> dplyr::count(value_final, sort = TRUE) |>
    dplyr::rename(!!f := value_final, studies = n)
}
for (f in c("taxonomic_class", "conflict_type", "marine_terrestrial", "study_design")) {
  d <- .field_counts(f)
  if (is.null(d)) { cat("\n", f, ": excluded as unreliable\n"); next }
  print(knitr::kable(head(d, 20), caption = sprintf("%s (n = %d studies with a verified value)",
                                                    f, sum(d$studies))))
  save_tab(d, paste0("07_", f))
}

    save_tab(sp_map, "07_species_normalisation_audit")
  }

8 Robustness

Every headline count is recomputed under defensible changes of rule. A finding that flips is not a finding.

.recount <- function(d, label) {
  cl <- d |> tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::all_of(COUNTRIES), names_to = "country",
                                 values_to = "covered") |>
    dplyr::filter(covered %in% TRUE)
  tibble::tibble(variant = label, n_studies = NROW(d)) |>
    dplyr::bind_cols(as_tibble_row(setNames(
      vapply(COUNTRIES, function(c) sum(cl$country == c), integer(1)), COUNTRIES)))
}
# NOTE ON (a) AND (c). The protocol lists "union vs intersection decision
# rule" and "contested records included vs excluded" as separate variants. On
# this corpus they are the SAME set operation: a contested record is by
# definition one that exactly one model included, so dropping the contested
# set IS applying the intersection rule. They are computed once and labelled
# as one variant. Reporting them as two independent corroborations would
# double-count a single check, which is the opposite of what a robustness
# analysis is for.
variants <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  .recount(map, "headline (union rule, all)"),
  .recount(map |> dplyr::filter(!contested),
           "(a)=(c) intersection rule / contested excluded"),
  .recount(map |> dplyr::filter(max_confidence %in% "high"), "(b) high-confidence only"),
  .recount(map |> dplyr::filter(stratum == "peer-reviewed"), "(d) peer-reviewed only"),
  .recount(map |> dplyr::filter(tier != "C_asserted_no_evidence"),
           "(f) geographic tier C excluded"))
knitr::kable(variants, caption = "Studies per country under each robustness variant")
Studies per country under each robustness variant
variant n_studies Tunisia Algeria Morocco Libya Egypt
headline (union rule, all) 262 81 47 76 31 75
(a)=(c) intersection rule / contested excluded 73 24 11 23 4 19
(b) high-confidence only 252 79 46 75 31 74
(d) peer-reviewed only 198 63 41 61 28 64
(f) geographic tier C excluded 185 54 29 58 18 62 
save_tab(variants, "07_robustness_variants")
## # A tibble: 5 × 7
##   variant                          n_studies Tunisia Algeria Morocco Libya Egypt
##   <chr>                                <int>   <int>   <int>   <int> <int> <int>
## 1 headline (union rule, all)             262      81      47      76    31    75
## 2 (a)=(c) intersection rule / con…        73      24      11      23     4    19
## 3 (b) high-confidence only               252      79      46      75    31    74
## 4 (d) peer-reviewed only                 198      63      41      61    28    64
## 5 (f) geographic tier C excluded         185      54      29      58    18    62

Variants (a) and (c) are one variant, not two. A contested record is by definition one that exactly one model included, so excluding the contested set is the intersection rule. They are reported together; presenting them as two independent checks would double-count a single test.

The intersection rule cuts the map from 262 studies to 73 — it removes 72% of the evidence base. Variant (b) removes almost nothing (10 records), because 96% of includes were high-confidence. The classifier was confidently wrong, not tentatively wrong, so confidence filtering is not a usable safeguard here.

ranks <- variants |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::all_of(COUNTRIES), names_to = "country", values_to = "n") |>
  dplyr::group_by(variant) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rank = rank(-n, ties.method = "min")) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::select(variant, country, rank) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = variant, values_from = rank)
knitr::kable(ranks, caption = "Rank of each country under each variant. A stable ordering is the claim this map can defend.")

top_stable <- ranks |> dplyr::filter(dplyr::if_all(-country, ~ .x == 1))
bottom <- ranks |> dplyr::filter(dplyr::if_all(-country, ~ .x >= 4))

No country ranks first under every variant — the leading position is not robust and must not be reported as a finding. Algeria and Libya rank in the bottom two under every variant, which is the more robust half of the geographic finding: the map can defend where the evidence is thinnest more confidently than where it is densest.

9 What this map can and cannot conclude

n_frag <- sum(map$n_cells == 1)
n_tierC <- sum(map$tier == "C_asserted_no_evidence")
  • Defensible: the ordering of countries by research volume, to the extent the robustness table above shows it stable, and the fact that 59 in-scope records cannot be placed in any country at all.
  • Defensible with its qualifier: that research is thin in the low-count countries of the English-indexed literature reachable by this search.
  • Not defensible: any claim that a low count reflects an absence of research. 111 records hinge on a single search cell, 77 sit in the weakest geographic tier, zero records are in French or Arabic, and full text was unobtainable for 141 of 262 records.
